Two new community-led Catchment Action Plans are now in development: 🛠️ 
 
🌿 Inland Mata-Au/Clutha (from the Nevis and Lindis ranges through to Dunstan, Ida Valley, Manuherikia, Alexandra, Roxburgh, and Millers Flat) 
 
🌿 Lower Mata-Au/Clutha (from the Pomahaka through to Clinton, Balclutha, Beaumont, Milton, and the Taiari/Taieri Mouth)

Last week, more than 30 people gathered for the first Dunedin Coastal Catchments Integrated Catchment Group meeting, marking the start of creating a Catchment Action Plan for the area. 

The community, along with representatives from mana whenua, fishing, forestry, farming, conservation and many other sectors brought a wealth of knowledge, experience and local insight to the table. 

Together, we started exploring the values that matter most in this area — reflecting on how they looked in the past, how they look today and what we want future generations to inherit. 

There was real enthusiasm for working together across communities, projects and priorities to achieve better environmental outcomes; there is a shared commitment to the long-term health and wellbeing of our environment and communities. 🙌 

Wait — what’s a Catchment Action Plan? 🤔 

A catchment is an area where all water flows to the same river, lake, or coastline, and a Catchment Action Plan defines the area of the catchment or connected catchments the community will focus on.   

These plans take a whole-of-catchment approach to caring for our environment, from the mountains to the sea (ki uta ki tai). They build on the great work already being done by iwi, communities, catchment groups and local government, helping coordinate efforts across fresh water, land, soils, coastal environments and the values that matter most to local people.  
 
Because what happens upstream affects everything downstream, environmental issues need to be tackled together rather than in isolation. 

Check out the work enhancing the Dunedin Coastal areas:

#haveyoursay #public #localgovernment #governmentreform #otago #otagomayoralforum","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/otago-regional-council_haveyoursay-public-localgovernment-activity-7469538691611291648-U0u2"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Otago Regional Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/otago-regional-council"},"datePublished":"2026-05-22T04:30:16.002Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/otago-regional-council_internationaldayforbiodiversity-biodiversity-activity-7463446106945900544-mCVJ","text":"If you think Otago’s species are just penguins, sea lions and albatross ... think again!

It’s International Day for Biodiversity, a day where we celebrate the rich diversity of life that makes our world — including Otago — so special. 
 
We’re proud to be home to hundreds of unique species, many of which are regionally endemic, meaning they ONLY naturally occur and breed in Otago — and nowhere else in the world. That makes protecting their environment not just important, but essential. 

We’re shining a spotlight on three regionally endemic species you may have never heard of: 

🪲 The Alexandra chafer beetle — a flightless, blackish longhorn beetle, found only in the close vicinity of Alexandra. 
 
🦎 The schist gecko — a brilliantly camouflaged species of lizard that lives in tors and outcrops of schist rock only in Central Otago.  
 
🌼Myosotis oreophila — a diminutive forget-me-not, plant species that is only found in rocky, high-elevation blocks of schist habitats in Central Otago.  

Let’s keep working together to protect our land, waterways, and ultimately the habitats for our diverse species — for today, for tomorrow, and for generations to come. 💪 

Check out the unique species we have in Otago: 
👉 orc.govt.nz/endemic

#internationaldayforbiodiversity #biodiversity #environment #nativespecies ##endemicspecies #regionallyendemicspecies #otago ","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/otago-regional-council_internationaldayforbiodiversity-biodiversity-activity-7463446106945900544-mCVJ"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Otago Regional Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/otago-regional-council"},"datePublished":"2026-05-01T03:50:01.974Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/otago-regional-council_mataau-clutha-inlandclutha-activity-7455825836626178048-8hF0","text":"Help plan a future for the Mata-Au/Clutha’s environment! 🏞️ 
 
We're forming two groups with action plans; the Inland Mata-Au Clutha and the Lower Mata-Au Clutha — and we want you to be part of it. 🙌 
 
The two groups are: 
• Inland Mata-Au/Clutha catchment group — covering Nevis and Lindis to Dunstan, Ida Valley and Manuherekia to Alexandra and through Roxburgh to Millers Flat. 
• Lower Mata-Au/Clutha catchment group — covering the Pomahaka, Clinton and Balclutha, Beaumont to Milton and along the coast from Mata-Au/Clutha Mouth to Toko Mouth and up to Taiari/Taieri Mouth. 
 
You can check out the boundary maps below. 
 
These two groups will help guide practical, on-the-ground action for each area — the catchment action plan. 
 
What’s the catchment action plan? 
 
It focuses on the management and conservation of ecosystems across an entire catchment area, from the mountains to the sea (ki uta ki tai). It builds on the work that iwi, communities, catchment groups and local government are already doing to protect and manage their place.

Our Dunedin-based teams are now all together in one central location at 180 High Street, Dunedin. This modern, accessible space makes it easier for you to connect with us for all customer services, including Orbus enquiries, with on-site parking and improved access to council services. 

It’s not just a building – it’s a space with meaning. The cultural design work at Aonui is inspired by mana whenua whakapapa and histories, together with features of the local environment. 

The name Aonui, endorsed by kā Rūnaka across the region, reflects values of kaitiakitaka, rakatirataka, manaakitaka and te mana o te wai — expressing care for the environment, inclusive leadership, and the protection of freshwater for future generations. 

In Kāi Tahu tradition, Aonui is linked to the pursuit of knowledge in the natural world and is reflected in local landmarks, including a basaltic pillar north of the Tokomairaro River. The site also has historical connections to the Toitū awa, a stream that once flowed through the area. 

Bringing our teams together in a space of both practicality and cultural significance helps us work more efficiently while honouring our commitment to the environment and mana whenua. 

Our regional offices and depots across Otago remain unchanged.  

We look forward to seeing you soon at Aonui! 👋 ","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/otago-regional-council_our-dunedin-offices-have-moved-welcome-activity-7455375379416043520-xu1U"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Otago Regional Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/otago-regional-council"},"datePublished":"2026-04-21T22:00:04.277Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/otago-regional-council_wilddunedin-nzfestivalofnature-talk-activity-7452476275094495232-EGhV","text":"Shout out to catchment advisor Janice! 👏 
 
She recently took to the stage at one of the talks during the Wild Dunedin festival to share how we can all be kaitiaki (guardians) for our urban streams. 

Janice’s talk, ‘From Street to Streams: Caring for our urban waterways', was about the link between our urban stormwater systems and the incredible biodiversity living in our local backyard. 💧 

Unlike the water from your sink or shower, stormwater is not treated. It flows through our drains and carries whatever it picks up on the ground — oil, litter or detergents — straight into our waterways. 🌊 

From uni students to local legends in their 70s, it was inspiring to see so many people wanting to learn more about our biodiversity and how to protect it. One attendee even shared a tearful "thank you" for the work being done — a reminder of just how much waterways and the life teeming within them mean to our community. 🤝👩‍👩‍👧‍👦 

No matter where you are in Otago (or anywhere in Aotearoa New Zealand), we all have a part to play in keeping our waterways and biodiversity thriving. 🙌

        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary"> ✨ Mānawatia a Matariki — Welcome Matariki ✨ 

Ka puta a Matariki, ka rere a Whānui. Ko te tohu tēnā o te tau hou Māori. 

Matariki appears, Whānui rises. That is the sign of the Māori New Year. 

Matariki is signalled by the rising of the Matariki star cluster in the winter sky over Aotearoa New Zealand. 

This time invites you to remember loved ones, celebrate the present and plan for the promising year ahead. 

This year’s theme is Matariki herenga waka — it is all about inclusion and encouraging all people to celebrate Matariki together. The theme has strong connections to multi-culturalism and the sharing of cultural practices. 

Whether it's sharing kai, remembering loved ones, reflecting on the past, setting new goals, or simply spending time together, celebrate Matariki in a way that feels right for you. 

From all of us at Otago Regional Council, we wish you a meaningful Matariki. 

Nau mai, haere mai — join us in celebrating the Māori New Year. 🥳

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Exciting progress is underway for the Mata-Au/Clutha catchments! 

Two new community-led Catchment Action Plans are now in development: 🛠️ 
 
🌿 Inland Mata-Au/Clutha (from the Nevis and Lindis ranges through to Dunstan, Ida Valley, Manuherikia, Alexandra, Roxburgh, and Millers Flat) 
 
🌿 Lower Mata-Au/Clutha (from the Pomahaka through to Clinton, Balclutha, Beaumont, Milton, and the Taiari/Taieri Mouth) 

The first workshops were held last week in Cromwell and Tapanui, bringing together members of each planning group for the first time.  

The workshops gave participants the opportunity to get to know one another, learn about the Catchment Action Plan process, explore the environmental values that matter most in their local catchments, and begin building a shared vision for the work ahead. 

Both plans are facilitated by our Integrated Catchment Management team and codeveloped by local communities, with each group focused on the needs and priorities of their own catchment. 

A huge thank you to everyone who has volunteered their time, local knowledge and experience. 

We look forward to working alongside both groups over the coming months! 🤝 

Each group will take part in six workshops to develop their plans, which are expected to be completed in early 2027. 

There will also be opportunities for the wider community to have their say through surveys and other engagement activities, so keep an eye on this page for updates. 

If you'd like to stay informed or learn more about how you can be involved as the plans move towards delivery, get in touch with our Integrated Catchment Management team at:

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">One room, 30+ locals and a massive vision for the Dunedin and coastal environment. ✨ 

Last week, more than 30 people gathered for the first Dunedin Coastal Catchments Integrated Catchment Group meeting, marking the start of creating a Catchment Action Plan for the area. 

The community, along with representatives from mana whenua, fishing, forestry, farming, conservation and many other sectors brought a wealth of knowledge, experience and local insight to the table. 

Together, we started exploring the values that matter most in this area — reflecting on how they looked in the past, how they look today and what we want future generations to inherit. 

There was real enthusiasm for working together across communities, projects and priorities to achieve better environmental outcomes; there is a shared commitment to the long-term health and wellbeing of our environment and communities. 🙌 

Wait — what’s a Catchment Action Plan? 🤔 

A catchment is an area where all water flows to the same river, lake, or coastline, and a Catchment Action Plan defines the area of the catchment or connected catchments the community will focus on.   

These plans take a whole-of-catchment approach to caring for our environment, from the mountains to the sea (ki uta ki tai). They build on the great work already being done by iwi, communities, catchment groups and local government, helping coordinate efforts across fresh water, land, soils, coastal environments and the values that matter most to local people.  
 
Because what happens upstream affects everything downstream, environmental issues need to be tackled together rather than in isolation.

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">If you think Otago’s species are just penguins, sea lions and albatross ... think again!

It’s International Day for Biodiversity, a day where we celebrate the rich diversity of life that makes our world — including Otago — so special. 
 
We’re proud to be home to hundreds of unique species, many of which are regionally endemic, meaning they ONLY naturally occur and breed in Otago — and nowhere else in the world. That makes protecting their environment not just important, but essential. 

We’re shining a spotlight on three regionally endemic species you may have never heard of: 

🪲 The Alexandra chafer beetle — a flightless, blackish longhorn beetle, found only in the close vicinity of Alexandra. 
 
🦎 The schist gecko — a brilliantly camouflaged species of lizard that lives in tors and outcrops of schist rock only in Central Otago.  
 
🌼Myosotis oreophila — a diminutive forget-me-not, plant species that is only found in rocky, high-elevation blocks of schist habitats in Central Otago.  

Let’s keep working together to protect our land, waterways, and ultimately the habitats for our diverse species — for today, for tomorrow, and for generations to come. 💪 

Check out the unique species we have in Otago:

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Help plan a future for the Mata-Au/Clutha’s environment! 🏞️ 
 
We're forming two groups with action plans; the Inland Mata-Au Clutha and the Lower Mata-Au Clutha — and we want you to be part of it. 🙌 
 
The two groups are: 
• Inland Mata-Au/Clutha catchment group — covering Nevis and Lindis to Dunstan, Ida Valley and Manuherekia to Alexandra and through Roxburgh to Millers Flat. 
• Lower Mata-Au/Clutha catchment group — covering the Pomahaka, Clinton and Balclutha, Beaumont to Milton and along the coast from Mata-Au/Clutha Mouth to Toko Mouth and up to Taiari/Taieri Mouth. 
 
You can check out the boundary maps below. 
 
These two groups will help guide practical, on-the-ground action for each area — the catchment action plan. 
 
What’s the catchment action plan? 
 
It focuses on the management and conservation of ecosystems across an entire catchment area, from the mountains to the sea (ki uta ki tai). It builds on the work that iwi, communities, catchment groups and local government are already doing to protect and manage their place. 
 
Come along in person or join us online to learn more about each group and how you can get involved: 
 
✨ Inland Mata-Au/Clutha ✨ 
 
🗓️In-person info session on Monday, 11 May:  
Alexandra Community House (14/20 Centennial Avenue, Alexandra) 
3.30–4.30pm 
  
👨💻Online (via Zoom) on Monday,11 May: 
6.30–7.30pm 
Join via Zoom 👉 <a class="link" href="http://orc.govt.nz/inlandcapzoom?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" rel="nofollow" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>orc.govt.nz/inlandcapzoom</a> 
 
✨ Lower Mata-Au/Clutha ✨ 
  
🗓️In-person info session on Tuesday, 12 May:  
Cross Recreation Centre (18 Glasgow Street, Balclutha) 
3.30–4.30pm 
  
👨💻Online (via Zoom) on Monday, 18 May: 
6.30–7.30pm

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Our Dunedin offices have moved – welcome to Aonui! 📍 

Our Dunedin-based teams are now all together in one central location at 180 High Street, Dunedin. This modern, accessible space makes it easier for you to connect with us for all customer services, including Orbus enquiries, with on-site parking and improved access to council services. 

It’s not just a building – it’s a space with meaning. The cultural design work at Aonui is inspired by mana whenua whakapapa and histories, together with features of the local environment. 

The name Aonui, endorsed by kā Rūnaka across the region, reflects values of kaitiakitaka, rakatirataka, manaakitaka and te mana o te wai — expressing care for the environment, inclusive leadership, and the protection of freshwater for future generations. 

In Kāi Tahu tradition, Aonui is linked to the pursuit of knowledge in the natural world and is reflected in local landmarks, including a basaltic pillar north of the Tokomairaro River. The site also has historical connections to the Toitū awa, a stream that once flowed through the area. 

Bringing our teams together in a space of both practicality and cultural significance helps us work more efficiently while honouring our commitment to the environment and mana whenua. 

Our regional offices and depots across Otago remain unchanged.  

We look forward to seeing you soon at Aonui! 👋 </p>

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Shout out to catchment advisor Janice! 👏 
 
She recently took to the stage at one of the talks during the Wild Dunedin festival to share how we can all be kaitiaki (guardians) for our urban streams. 

Janice’s talk, ‘From Street to Streams: Caring for our urban waterways', was about the link between our urban stormwater systems and the incredible biodiversity living in our local backyard. 💧 

Unlike the water from your sink or shower, stormwater is not treated. It flows through our drains and carries whatever it picks up on the ground — oil, litter or detergents — straight into our waterways. 🌊 

From uni students to local legends in their 70s, it was inspiring to see so many people wanting to learn more about our biodiversity and how to protect it. One attendee even shared a tearful "thank you" for the work being done — a reminder of just how much waterways and the life teeming within them mean to our community. 🤝👩👩👧👦 

No matter where you are in Otago (or anywhere in Aotearoa New Zealand), we all have a part to play in keeping our waterways and biodiversity thriving. 🙌

        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Help plan a future for Dunedin’s environment! 🏞️

We need your help to create a catchment action plan for the Dunedin Coastal catchment (check out the boundary map below). 

What’s a catchment action plan? 🤔

It focuses on the management and conservation of ecosystems across an entire catchment area, from the mountains to the sea (ki uta ki tai). It builds on the work that iwi, communities, catchment groups and local government are already doing to protect and manage their place. 

The plan covers freshwater and saltwater environments, along with land, soils and key community values. 

And you can get involved! 🙋♂️
